title: Incremental capacity fastpath + physical GPU swap runbook (draft)
content:
Purpose and scope:
This is a practical fastpath runbook for oncall SREs to:
- replace a failed GPU on a host with minimal service disruption,
- cordon/drain an unhealthy node safely,
- perform a rapid cluster recovery when multiple pods are impacted, and
- inject incremental capacity (burst nodes/GPU instances) to stabilize latency SLOs.

Audience and assumptions:
- Audience: primary oncall, secondary oncall, oncall lead for escalations.
- Assumes access to cloud console (GCP/AWS account), Datadog, PagerDuty, Slack #sre-duty, and ticketing (JIRA OPS team).
- Assumes automated deployment jobs are configured and images are tested; the cluster is k8s 1.26+ with cluster-autoscaler in place.

High level decision matrix (quick):
- Single pod GPU error on node, node still Healthy: try pod restart -> if same error, cordon+drain node and evict pods; schedule replacement.
- Node kernel panic or unreachable: cordon node, drain with graceful timeout=30s if low-latency routes; otherwise force-evict after 90s.
- Multiple nodes showing GPU ECC/fatal errors: consider cluster-wide degraded mode, inject capacity and enable cpu-only fallbacks for non-critical traffic.
- If cluster CPU/GPU utilization >85% for sustained 5m and p50 latency > twice SLO: trigger capacity-add fastpath.

Primary contacts and escalation flow:
- Oncall SRE (first responder) -> use template runbook below.
- Secondary SRE (escalation after 20m or earlier if unsure): Marco Ruiz.
- Hardware specialist / Solutions Eng: Chen Li.
- PagerDuty escalation policy: urgent if model-serving 5xx >0.5% or p99 latency >3x SLO for more than 10m.

Preflight checks (before touching anything):
- Confirm the incident with metrics: Datadog dashboard (service:inference, env:prod)
  - tokens/sec, request rate, p50/p95/p99 latency, 5xx rate.
- Check cluster health: kubectl get nodes -o wide | grep NotReady
- Review recent deploys: look for GH Actions or CI runs within last 30m.
- Post to #sre-duty with short summary, current impact, and runbook step being attempted.

Commands snippet (copy/paste carefully):
- Show GPU driver / pods using GPUs: kubectl get pods -o=custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,NODE:.spec.nodeName,RESOURCES:.spec.containers[*].resources --all-namespaces | grep gpu
- Describe node: kubectl describe node <node-name>
- Check kubelet/journal logs: ssh node && sudo journalctl -u kubelet -n 300 --no-pager
- Check GPU health (NVIDIA): ssh node && sudo nvidia-smi -q | egrep "(Fan Speed|Temperature|ECC|Compute Mode|Driver Version)" -A3

Fast GPU-swap procedure (physical or cloud instance ephemeral GPU):
1) Quick verification (5 mins):
   - Validate pod failures reference GPU errors (OOM/driver/kubelet eviction vs app error).
   - Note impacted model versions and traffic % (Datadog service tags).
2) Reroute traffic if necessary (immediate mitigation):
   - If traffic >30% impacted: use runtime routing to send new requests to fallback model variant (see console route: inference-route/fallback) or scale up cpu-only workers.
3) Cordon node: kubectl cordon <node>
   - Annotation: add: kubectl annotate node <node> redwood/sre-maintenance=true --overwrite
4) Drain node with staged eviction:
   - kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=30 --timeout=5m
   - Watch for stuck pods: kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node>
   - If pods stuck >5m: escalate to secondary SRE and consider force deletion: kubectl delete pod <pod> --grace-period=0 --force
5) Replace GPU / reprovision host:
   - If cloud GPU (preemptible/spot): trigger new instance from capacity group or use autoscaler. For dedicated hosts, follow hardware swap SOP (see notes below).
   - For physical replacements: coordinate maintenance window with oncall lead. Use ticket JIRA-OPS-4123 for asset tracking.
6) Validate new node:
   - Wait until node Ready and GPU visible: kubectl get nodes && nvidia-smi on host.
   - Re-enable scheduling: kubectl uncordon <node>
   - Confirm pods schedule back and pass health checks.
7) Post-checks (15-30 mins):
   - Monitor p50/p95/p99 and 5xx. Rollback traffic routing if stable for 10m.

Cluster recovery when multiple pods/nodes impacted:
- Trigger partial degraded mode: adjust Canary/traffic-split to serve critical customers only.
- Add capacity: run capacity fastpath (steps below).
- If control plane degraded (api-server high 5xx): check etcd health and control-plane nodes; do not mass-delete pods. Contact infra lead immediately.

Capacity-add (fastpath) checklist:
- Use policy: if sustained queueing latency >300ms for 3 consecutive minutes AND node-level GPU utilization >80% -> add +20% GPUs (minimum 2 instances).
- Steps to add capacity: create temporary instance group (GCE) or launch cluster-autoscaler scale-up with annotation: kubectl apply -f temp-nodepool-scaleup.yaml (prefilled template in GH repo).
- Tag new nodes with redwood/ephemeral:true and taint if needed: kubectl taint nodes <name> critical=ephemeral:NoSchedule
- Drain and migrate low-priority workloads away from new nodes until ready.
- Verify autoscaler and HPA interactions.

Quick rollback and safety knobs:
- If new capacity causes regression (higher p99 or 5xx): cut traffic to new nodes by removing node labels used in routing OR scale down the pool.
- Use runtime feature gate to disable fallback model routing if it increases error rate.
- If a kernel panic correlates with a specific kernel version, pin nodes to previous image and roll out with maxUnavailable=1.

Observability checklist to record in incident ticket:
- Attach Datadog graphs (CPU/GPU utilization, queue depth, latency).
- Paste condensed kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp | tail -n 200
- Add nvidia-smi output, kubelet logs, and relevant kernel oops if present.
- Note exact times of cordon/drain/uncordon and pod evictions.

Postmortem prompts (short list to populate later):
- What was the root cause? hardware, driver, kernel, thermal, or app-level?
- Did autoscaler react fast enough? If not, why?
- What mitigations prevented customer impact, and what failed?
- Action items: automated detection for ECC/fatal GPU errors, standardized cordon+annotate script, prebuilt capacity templates for region X, recovery runbook training.

Running exercises and testing ideas (notes to self):
- Run quarterly chaos test: simulate a single GPU failing while running a heavy model for 10m. Observe failover time.
- Add a scripted CLI: redwood-sre node-maintenance --node <node> --reason "gpu-failure" that performs cordon->drain->annotate with checkpoints.
- Bake in health-check sidecar to detect driver-level errors before kubelet reports NotReady.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Should we make default drain grace-period 60s for model-serving pods? Current 30s sometimes cuts token streams mid-response.
- Need a lightweight traffic-splitting API for emergency fallback that ops can call without console access.
- Confirm which oncall role gets notified on hardware warranty requests.

Appendix: useful commands and templates
- Annotated cordon+drain script (local):
  #!/bin/bash
  NODE=$1
  REASON=$2
  kubectl annotate node $NODE redwood/sre-maintenance="$REASON" --overwrite
  kubectl cordon $NODE
  kubectl drain $NODE --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=30 --timeout=5m

- temp-nodepool-scaleup.yaml (reference in repo): see https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/tree/main/templates

- Incident summary template to paste to JIRA:
  - Impact: (customers, % requests failed, duration)
  - Timeline: (timestamps of key actions)
  - Root cause hypothesis: (one line)
  - Actions taken: (list)
  - Next steps: (list)

Notes: this is intentionally concise and actionable. Keep iterations small; prefer automation where we repeatedly do identical sequences. Add improvements to GH PR: infra/runbooks/fastpath-node-maintenance.md

-- end of draft --

Editor notes: needs links to hardware SOP and warranty process; confirm retention policy for logs attached to tickets.
